title: Which favors will you deny?
hook: the refrain repeated thirty-one times: which of your Lord's favors will you deny (55:13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mizan, and your line was keep the balance. Did you make your one small correction? Day six hundred five.

The Prophet ﷺ once recited a whole surah to his companions, a report in Tirmidhi says, and they listened to the end in silence. Then he told them that another audience had answered it better. Not with silence: with words, every time a certain line came round. And the line came round a lot. In Surah Ar-Rahman, one question returns again and again, after fruit, after the seas, after the rising places of the sun. Today, that question, and who answered it.

Verse thirteen, the first of thirty-one times it appears. Pickthall: "Which is it, of the favours of your Lord, that ye deny?" In Arabic: fa-bi-ayyi ala'i rabbikuma tukadhdhiban. Two things are hidden in the grammar. First, rabbikuma, your Lord, and tukadhdhiban, you deny, are dual: they speak to two. Who are the two? Later in the surah, verse thirty-three addresses the company of jinn and humans, and commentators read the whole refrain as spoken to both. Second, ala'. Pickthall says favors, and that is the usual reading: blessings, bounties, gifts. Some commentators add that ala' can also carry the sense of wonders, signs of power. So the line asks two things at once: which of these gifts, and which of these marvels, will you call a lie? Notice that it's a question, not an accusation. The surah lists a gift, then stops and asks. Fruit and palm trees: which will you deny? The two seas and their pearls: which will you deny? Even warnings get the refrain, as if being warned were a kindness too. Now the report from the beginning. The better audience, the Prophet told his companions, was the jinn. Each time he reached the refrain, they replied that they denied none of their Lord's favors, and praise belonged to Him. Some listeners still answer the refrain that way under their breath. On this reading, the repetition isn't filler. It's a stop after every blessing, long enough to notice it.
screen: `FA-BI-AYYI ALA'I RABBIKUMA.` · `SPOKEN TO TWO: JINN AND HUMANS.` · `A QUESTION, NOT AN ACCUSATION.` · `THE JINN ANSWERED IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: say it after each blessing you notice. Sit, and breathe. Let one ordinary gift come to mind: the breath you're taking, the light in the room, someone who texted you this week. After each one, ask the question quietly: which of His favors? If you pray, you can answer the way the report says the jinn did, that you deny none of them. If you don't, simply name the gift and let it sit. Then the next one. The bell holds the time.
Which favors will you deny? The refrain of Surah Ar-Rahman, asked thirty-one times, to jinn and humans alike. Today's word.
screen: `WHICH FAVORS WILL YOU DENY? — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: which of his favors? Today, three times, when something good happens, ask it under your breath before you move on. Day six hundred five.

howItsDone: Surah Ar-Rahman is often recited aloud, and some Muslims, hearing the refrain, quietly answer that they deny none of their Lord's favors, following the report in Tirmidhi.

original.note: Arabic: so which of the favors of your Lord will you two deny? The dual endings speak to two.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line repeated for rhythm.
what it means: a question asked after every gift and warning, to stop and notice.
what a scholar hears: the dual rabbikuma and tukadhdhiban, read with 55:33 as jinn and humans; ala' as favors, and for some commentators, wondrous signs.
